title: The Origins of Islam
description: Muhammad and the early Muslim community

concepts.title: Pre-Islamic Arabia
concepts.contentHtml:
The Arabian Peninsula was home to nomadic and settled tribes, polytheistic religion, and trading cities (Mecca, Medina). Caravan routes carried goods from Yemen to the Mediterranean. Christian and Jewish communities lived among the polytheistic majority.

Roman/Byzantine and Sassanid Persian empires bordered Arabia. Constant Byzantine-Persian wars in the early 7th century weakened both — opening unprecedented opportunities for new powers.

concepts.title: Muhammad
concepts.contentHtml:
Muhammad ibn Abdullah (c. 570-632 CE) was born in Mecca. From age 40 he received what Muslims hold to be revelations from God (Allah) through the angel Gabriel — collected after his death as the Quran.

His monotheistic preaching met opposition in Mecca. The 622 CE migration (Hijra) to Medina marks the start of the Islamic calendar. There Muhammad consolidated political and religious authority.

By his death in 632, most of the Arabian Peninsula was Muslim and unified — an extraordinary transformation in two decades.

concepts.title: The Five Pillars
concepts.contentHtml:
Sunni Islam's Five Pillars structure devout Muslim life:

• Shahada: declaration of faith ('There is no god but God, and Muhammad is His messenger').
• Salah: prayer five times daily, facing Mecca.
• Zakat: charitable giving (~2.5% of wealth annually).
• Sawm: fasting during Ramadan.
• Hajj: pilgrimage to Mecca, at least once if able.

The Quran (revealed text) and Hadith (sayings/actions of Muhammad) form the religious basis. Islamic law (sharia) is derived from these sources via various jurisprudential schools.

title: Caliphates and Expansion
description: From Arabia to a vast empire

concepts.title: Rashidun and Umayyad
concepts.contentHtml:
After Muhammad's death, the Rashidun ('rightly guided') caliphs led rapid expansion. Within ~30 years, Muslim armies had conquered Sassanid Persia entirely and substantial Byzantine territory (Egypt, Syria, North Africa).

The Umayyad Caliphate (661-750), based in Damascus, extended the empire from Spain to Central Asia. By 750 the Umayyads ruled an area larger than the Roman Empire at its peak.

Conversion of conquered peoples to Islam was gradual; non-Muslim subjects (especially Christians and Jews) paid a special tax (jizya) but had legal protection as 'people of the book'.

concepts.title: Sunni-Shia Split
concepts.contentHtml:
The split between Sunni and Shia Muslims originated in disputes over leadership succession after Muhammad. Sunnis (~90% of Muslims today) accepted the consensus-elected caliphs. Shia (~10%) held that Muhammad's son-in-law Ali and his descendants were the rightful leaders.

Ali was murdered in 661 CE; his son Husayn was killed at Karbala in 680 CE — a defining tragedy in Shia memory.

The split has theological and ritual differences but is also a major axis of modern political conflict (Iran-Saudi rivalry, sectarian violence in Iraq, Lebanon, Yemen).

concepts.title: Abbasid Golden Age
concepts.contentHtml:
The Abbasid Caliphate (750-1258) shifted the capital to Baghdad — for centuries the world's largest and most cosmopolitan city. The 'Islamic Golden Age' saw extraordinary intellectual achievement.

The House of Wisdom in Baghdad translated Greek, Persian, Indian texts into Arabic — preserving classical learning while building on it. Scholars like al-Khwarizmi (algebra, algorithms), Ibn Sina (medicine), al-Razi (chemistry), al-Haytham (optics) made foundational contributions.

The Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258 ended the Abbasid era, but Islamic civilization continued to flourish in regional centers.

concepts.title: The Ottoman Empire
concepts.contentHtml:
The Ottomans rose from a small Turkish state in northwest Anatolia. Mehmed II conquered Constantinople in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire and renaming the city Istanbul.

At its peak under Suleiman the Magnificent (1520-66), the Ottoman Empire extended from Vienna to Yemen and from Algeria to Iran. It was a Sunni state with diverse subjects: Christians, Jews, Sufis, sectarian minorities, all governed under the millet system.

Decline accelerated through the 18th-19th centuries — losing wars to Russia, the Habsburgs, then to nationalist revolts (Greek, Serbian, Romanian, Bulgarian). Defeat in WWI ended the empire; modern Turkey emerged in 1923 under Mustafa Kemal Atatürk.

concepts.title: The Safavids
concepts.contentHtml:
The Safavid Empire (1501-1736) made Twelver Shia Islam the state religion of Persia (Iran), distinguishing it from its Sunni neighbors. The Safavids fostered Persian art, architecture (Isfahan's stunning mosques and palaces), and literature.

The Safavid-Ottoman rivalry was both political (border wars over Iraq) and religious (Sunni-Shia tension). It set the religious geography of the modern Middle East.

Iran is still distinctively Shia — about 90% of its population, contrasted with the predominantly Sunni Arab world.

concepts.title: The Mughals
concepts.contentHtml:
The Mughal Empire (1526-1858) ruled most of the Indian subcontinent at its peak. Founded by Babur, expanded by Akbar (a notable proponent of religious tolerance), reached its height under Shah Jahan (builder of the Taj Mahal) and Aurangzeb.

Hindu majority ruled by a Muslim minority. Akbar's policies of inclusion gave way to Aurangzeb's stricter Sunni orthodoxy. Mughal art, architecture, and Indo-Persian high culture endure.

British conquest reduced the Mughals to figureheads in the 18th century. The 1857 'Indian Mutiny' or first war of independence ended the dynasty; the British Crown took direct rule of India.

title: Modern Middle East
description: Imperial collapse to nation-states to current crises

concepts.title: WWI and Mandate Era
concepts.contentHtml:
WWI ended Ottoman rule. The 1916 Sykes-Picot Agreement secretly carved up Ottoman Arab lands between Britain and France; the 1917 Balfour Declaration committed Britain to a Jewish national home in Palestine.

The post-war 'mandate' system put Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, Palestine, Jordan under British or French rule. Borders were drawn for European convenience, often setting up future conflicts.

Independence followed in stages — Egypt formally 1922, Iraq 1932, Syria/Lebanon 1943-46, Israel 1948, Jordan 1946. Saudi Arabia (1932) and Iran (continuously) avoided mandate status.

concepts.title: Arab-Israeli Conflicts
concepts.contentHtml:
Jewish migration to British Palestine grew before and especially during WWII. The 1947 UN partition plan was rejected by Arab states. Israel declared independence May 1948; the resulting Arab-Israeli war ended with Israeli victory and ~700,000 Palestinians displaced (the Nakba).

Wars in 1956 (Suez), 1967 (Six-Day War, Israel takes West Bank, Gaza, Sinai, Golan), 1973 (Yom Kippur). Egyptian-Israeli peace 1979; Jordanian-Israeli peace 1994.

The Israeli-Palestinian conflict remains unresolved. The 2023-25 Gaza war is among the most recent and most destructive phases.

concepts.title: Iran, Iraq, the Gulf
concepts.contentHtml:
The 1979 Iranian Revolution overthrew the Shah and established the Islamic Republic — the first modern theocratic state. Iran's Shia identity, US-Iran rupture (Tehran embassy hostage crisis), and ideological export reshaped regional politics.

Iran-Iraq War (1980-88): ~500,000 deaths, no decisive outcome. The Persian Gulf War (1991) expelled Iraq from Kuwait. The 2003 US invasion of Iraq toppled Saddam Hussein but unleashed sectarian war.

'Arab Spring' (from 2010) toppled some autocrats (Tunisia, Egypt, Libya, Yemen) and led to civil wars in Syria and Yemen. The region remains in flux.

concepts.title: Islam's Global Geography
concepts.contentHtml:
~1.9 billion Muslims today — about 24% of humanity. The largest Muslim populations are in Indonesia, Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, Nigeria — most outside the Arab world.

Islam is the world's fastest-growing major religion, projected to surpass Christianity in adherents around 2050. Conversion plus relatively higher birthrates drive growth.

Sunni:Shia split is roughly 85:15 globally. Major Shia populations: Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Yemen, Bahrain, parts of South Asia. Most Sunni Muslims live in South and Southeast Asia.

concepts.title: Reform Movements
concepts.contentHtml:
Islamic intellectual and political movements span a wide spectrum:

• Modernist/reformist: Muhammad Abduh, Sir Sayyid Ahmad Khan emphasized engagement with modern knowledge.
• Fundamentalist/Salafi: literal Quran/Hadith readings; rejection of innovation. Saudi Wahhabism is one variant.
• Islamist political movements: Muslim Brotherhood, AKP in Turkey — combining Islamic identity with democratic participation.
• Extremist groups: Al-Qaeda, ISIS — minority but consequential.

The vast majority of Muslims are mainstream practitioners far from the political extremes.

concepts.title: 21st Century Challenges
concepts.contentHtml:
Population pressures, water scarcity (Middle East and North Africa are mostly arid), youth unemployment, governance challenges. Several states have fragile institutions.

Energy transitions threaten oil-dependent economies. Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 attempts massive economic diversification.

Increasing assertiveness in global affairs — Saudi Arabia, UAE, Iran, Turkey, Egypt all play larger geopolitical roles than 30 years ago. The Islamic world's relationship with the West, with East Asia, and within itself will continue to shape the 21st century.
